title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length \(n\ge 2\), outputs an integer D with \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using worst-case time \(n^{1+o(1)}\)?
definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with \(w=B_{\varepsilon}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer \(B_{\varepsilon}\); unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there is one algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\), and for every rational \(\eta >0\) there are constants \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta},N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) such that every execution on every pair of total length \(n\ge N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) uses at most \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta} n^{1+\eta}\) operations. \(A_{\varepsilon}\) halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\); the algorithm may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but not on \(\eta\). All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) or effective procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) from \(\varepsilon\) is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Determine whether worst-case sequence alignment can simultaneously achieve arbitrarily small fixed relative error and a time exponent approaching one.

importance.reason: A central accuracy–runtime frontier for sequence comparison, with recent work on each side of the tradeoff. It is a genuinely stronger near-exact runtime target than TCS-7220, retained under the user’s explicit acceptance of related edit-distance questions.

progress.text: Andoni–Nosatzki establish constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for every fixed \(\eta >0\).
Mao–Rubinstein give approximation schemes in quasi-strongly subquadratic time; this is not a near-linear bound.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its \(n^{1+o(1)}\) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy \(\varepsilon\), one algorithm must meet \(n^{1+\eta}\) bounds for every fixed \(\eta >0\) once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each \(\eta\), with uncontrolled dependence on \(\eta\), is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for each fixed \(\eta\). Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.
